Time_Annotation: Initially an area of thunderstorms formed west of Luzon late on August 26, possibly due to the remains of former Tropical Depression Jolina. Late on August 28 it formed into a tropical depression about 300 miles (480 km) south-southwest of Hong Kong. It moved west-northwest over northeastern Hainan late on August 29, before becoming a tropical storm 24 hours later. Early on August 31, the tropical storm began to drift north towards China. That evening, it struck Dongxing before weakening back into a tropical depression on September 1 and dissipating the following day.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Early on August 31, the tropical storm began to drift north towards China. Excessive rains fell in mainland China, with locations in Changjiang county measuring up to 831.1 mm in the 3 day period ending late on August 31.
Main_Event_Annotation: It moved west-northwest over northeastern Hainan late on August 29, before becoming a tropical storm 24 hours later.
Hazards_Annotation: Excessive rains fell in mainland China, with locations in Changjiang county measuring up to 831.1 mm in the 3 day period ending late on August 31. In all, 3680 houses were nearly destroyed, four died, and 3.5 million people were impacted by the tropical storm.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Upon JTWC's declaration of Tropical Depression 31W on November 3, a tropical storm warning was issued for Chuuk Lagoon, Losap, and Poluwat in the Federated States of Micronesia. Further west, Faraulep, Satawal, and Woleai were placed under a typhoon watch while Fananu and Ulul were placed under a tropical storm watch. As Haiyan intensified into a typhoon on November 5, warnings were raised across Yap State.

Much of the islands of Koror and Kayangel in Palau were placed under a typhoon watch. The government issued a mandatory evacuation for Kayangel, and although most residents ignored the warning, they all survived the storm. As Haiyan intensified into a typhoon on November 5, warnings were raised across Palau. Government offices in Melekeok were used as an evacuation building for Palau. Despite mandatory evacuation orders, most residents on Kayangel remained on the island and rode out the typhoon.

Time_Annotation: The article notes that meteorologist Ivan Ray Tannehill began tracking the storm on September 28 during the 1938 season review and later, a 2014 study by Chenoweth concluded that the storm actually formed over the southwestern Caribbean on September 25. It also states that the cyclone moved ashore Newfoundland near the Burin Peninsula on October 7.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text mentions landfall in the Yucatán Peninsula south of Tulum (Mexico), heavy rains and floods in western Cuba, passage just south of the Florida Keys with observations from Key West and Titusville (United States), movement towards the western Bahamas crossing the Abaco Islands, and finally moving ashore Newfoundland near the Burin Peninsula (Canada). It also references an alternate track striking Nicaragua.
Main_Event_Annotation: The article details the system weakening to a tropical depression before re-intensifying into a tropical storm in the Gulf of Mexico, and it peaked with winds of 60 mph – consistent with a Tropical Storm/Cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Hazard evidence includes heavy rains causing floods in western Cuba (leading to crop losses and destruction of dwellings) as well as the storm’s peak wind speeds (60 mph recorded along with sustained winds in Key West and Titusville), indicating both flood and wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: The track for this system begins over the northwestern Caribbean on October 2, and after moving inland the system rapidly weakened, dissipating over northern Louisiana on October 7.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm struck the Yucatán Peninsula on October 4 (implying Mexico) and made landfall in Galveston, Texas before dissipating over northern Louisiana on October 7 (implying United States).
Main_Event_Annotation: After emerging into the Gulf of Mexico early on October 5, the storm quickly re-strengthened into a tropical storm; the Atlantic hurricane reanalysis project later concluded that the cyclone was, at most, a minimal tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Although there were no reports of gale‐force winds, records indicate sustained winds of 29–35 mph (47–56 km/h) in Louisiana and Texas.

Time_Annotation: On April 2, a large tropical disturbance formed, and the next day, it was named Hansella despite only being a tropical depression. On April 10, Hansella dissipated just northwest of Réunion.

Hazards_Annotation: Gusts on Rodrigues reached 180 km/h (110 mph), causing heavy damage to crops and houses (Wind), and the cyclone dropped 182 mm (7.2 in) of rainfall in 24 hours, which is indicative of Flood conditions.

Time_Annotation: The article states: 'The season runs throughout 2024, though most tropical cyclones typically develop between May and October. The season's first named storm, Ewiniar, developed on May 25, and eventually intensified into the first typhoon of the season, while the last named storm, Pabuk, dissipated on December 25.'
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text notes: 'Within the northwestern Pacific Ocean, there are two separate agencies that assign names to tropical cyclones... The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) will name a tropical cyclone if it has 10-minute sustained wind speeds of at least 65 km/h (40 mph)... The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) assigns names to tropical cyclones which move into or form as a tropical depression in the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR)... Tropical depressions that are monitored by the United States' Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) are given a number with a "W" suffix.'

Time_Annotation: The article states, 'The Pacific typhoon season began on May 23, when a tropical storm named Ewiniar formed southeast of Palau,' and later notes, 'On June 6, another extratropical cyclone would absorb the remnants of Ewiniar, just off the coast of Alaska.'

Hazards_Annotation: Based on the classification of Yagi as a tropical storm/typhoon and referring to the Main_Event--Hazard table for Tropical Storm/Cyclone events, the associated hazards are Wind, Flood, and Lightning. The narrative supports this through mentions of strong winds, heavy rains and resulting floods.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Extensive F3 (although some localized F4) damage occurred to an entire square block of homes in the Crawford Street and Patterson Road subdivision. [5]
At the industrial complex (known as Molson Park), at least 15 other businesses were damaged or destroyed while one person died at a tire retreading facility. [7]
The tornado crossed Highway 400 at Essa Road, where the grandstand was heavily damaged and several barns nearby were destroyed, just missing the Barrie Racetrack. [7]
As it crossed the highway, the tornado moved into the Allandale subdivision where many homes sustained severe damage with much of their upper floors missing. [7]
On Briar Road, homes sustained only minor damage indicating some weakening of the tornado. [7]
Immediately to the east of Briar Road, Trillium Crescent sustained heavy damage indicating a temporary strengthening of the tornado. [7]
Four warehouses near Highway 11 were ripped apart. [5]
The tornado hit the Tollendal Woods and Minets Point area, taking out the Brentwood Marina and a nearby subdivision. [7]
In summary, the article reports that as many as 300 homes were damaged or destroyed in Barrie. [8]

On March 31, a separate tornado in western South Carolina attained F4 strength, killing seven people and injuring 30.
On April 15, a massive F4 tornado near Pearsall, Texas, killed five people and injured 12.

During the April 19–21 outbreak, Missouri experienced one death from tornadoes amid three F4 events.
During the April 19–21 outbreak, Arkansas experienced one death from tornadoes amid three F4 events.
Deadly F4 tornadoes in Oklahoma on May 24 and 26, with significant impacts to Keefton, killed a combined seven people.
A nighttime tornado ravaged Jonesboro, Arkansas on May 26, injuring nearly 300 people but resulting in only three deaths.
A long‐tracked, violent tornado crossed central Alabama on May 27, obliterating most of Brent and killing seven people.
A rare F4 tornado in New England on August 28 struck along the New York/Massachusetts state line, killing four people and injuring 36.
An outbreak sequence from September 24–26 in Kansas and Nebraska resulted in three deaths and almost 60 injuries.

On the latter date, an F2 tornado in the Parnell–Holbrook area in Iowa struck 25 farms in its path, tearing off roofs, leveling several barns, and causing one home to slide and buckle.[25]

Total_Summary_Deaths.Total_Deaths_Annotation: A total of 173 people were confirmed to have died as a result of the fires. The figure was originally estimated at 14 on the night of 7 February, and steadily increased over the following two weeks to 210. It was feared that it could rise as high as 240–280, but these figures were later revised down to 173 after further forensic examinations of remains, and after several missing people were located.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: On 11 February, fire authorities estimated that as many as 100 of Marysville's 519 residents could have perished.
The final death toll for Marysville was later downgraded to 34 after a large group of residents who remained unaccounted for were officially located.
Among the dead in the Kinglake West area were former Seven Network and Nine Network television personality Brian Naylor, and his wife Moiree.
Veteran TV actor Reg Evans and his partner, artist Angela Brunton, residing on a small farm in the St Andrews area, also died in the Kinglake area fire.
Ornithologist Richard Zann perished in the Kinglake fire, together with his wife Eileen and daughter Eva.

Time_Annotation: A small circulation formed north of the Cocos Islands on January 8 within the near-equatorial trough. A cold front swept Charly to the southeast, absorbing it on January 31.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The system produced convection that spread rainfall over Mauritius and Réunion.
Main_Event_Annotation: Early on January 21, Charly intensified into a tropical cyclone. Based on increased organization, the storm became an intense tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm reached peak 10-minute winds of 185 km/h (115 mph) and JTWC estimated peak 1-minute winds of 195 km/h (120 mph), indicating significant wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: Drifting to the southwest and later to the south, the associated convection waxed and waned, finally organizing more on April 4; on that day, the disturbance quickly intensified into Moderate Tropical Storm Evariste. On April 8, Evariste dissipated, dissipating ahead of the nearby trough.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: On April 6, increased wind shear turned Evariste to the south and it passed about 135 km east of St. Brandon, and on April 7, Evariste bypassed Rodrigues about 200 km to the southwest. Additionally, peak gusts were recorded on St. Brandon and stronger winds on Rodrigues.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system intensified into Moderate Tropical Storm Evariste, which places it in the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category as per the association table.
Hazards_Annotation: Evariste produced peak gusts of 91 km/h on St. Brandon and stronger winds reaching 109 km/h were recorded on Rodrigues, indicating wind as the primary hazard.

Event_Names: Deep Depression over Bay of Bengal, August 2016
Time_Annotation: A low-pressure area formed over the Bay of Bengal in mid-August 2016. It slowly consolidated, prompting the IMD to upgrade the system to a Depression on 16 August. The system slowly moved northwestward and intensified into a deep depression on the following day, before making landfall over the coast of West Bengal between Digha and Diamond Harbour.

Hazards_Annotation: The text mentions recorded winds of 70 km/h in Kolkata and heavy rainfall leading to flash flood concerns (with deployment of disaster response teams in Jharkhand), indicating hazards of both wind and flood.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In early August, Typhoon Lekima made landfall in China's Zhejiang province as a powerful typhoon, producing extensive rainfall and landslides that warranted over $9 billion worth of damages, making it, at the time, the second-costliest storm in Chinese history.

One month later, in early October, Typhoon Hagibis made landfall just west—at Shizuoka—as a large typhoon, causing extensive damages worth over $17 billion, making it, at that time, the costliest Pacific typhoon on record (unadjusted for inflation).

Time_Annotation: The season's first named storm, Pabuk, reached tropical storm status on January 1, and the season's last named storm, Phanfone, dissipated on December 29 after it made landfall in the Philippines.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: In early August, Typhoon Lekima made landfall in China's Zhejiang province; in September, Typhoon Faxai brushed Japan's Kantō region; and the Philippines experienced destructive impacts from Typhoon Kammuri and Typhoon Phanfone.
Main_Event_Annotation: The season produced a total of 29 named storms, 17 typhoons, and 5 super typhoons, indicating an active period of tropical cyclone activity.
Hazards_Annotation: The catastrophic impacts – including extensive rainfall, landslides, and destruction from strong winds as seen with Typhoon Lekima, Typhoon Faxai, and Typhoon Hagibis – align with the hazards (Wind, Flood, Lightning) associated with Tropical Storm/Cyclone events.

Time_Annotation: On August 1, a tropical depression formed to the east of Mariana Islands. By midnight on August 1, the depression rapidly intensified to be Tropical Storm Francisco. Main_Event_Annotation: By midnight on August 1, the depression rapidly intensified to be Tropical Storm Francisco. It then became a typhoon 12 hours later.
Hazards_Annotation: Striking Kyushu as a typhoon, Francisco brought heavy rain and strong winds to much of the island. Rainfall accumulations exceeded 120 mm (4.7 in) in Nobeoka and 110 mm (4.3 in) in Saiki. A maximum wind gust of 143 km/h (89 mph) was observed at Miyazaki Airport. One person drowned in a flooded river in Kokonoe. Two people suffered injury after being knocked over by strong winds.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In Cuba, heavy rainfall in Pinar del Río Province caused rivers and creeks to rise. However, only minimal damage was reported.[7]
On Estero Island, a number of buildings were damaged, including the casinos, cottages, and Crescent Beach resort.[8]
In Punta Rassa, the majority of homes were either extensively damaged or washed away.
At Ballast Point, the pavilion and bathhouse were destroyed by the storm.[19]
A total of 50 homes were destroyed by cedar logs used to construct cigar boxes at the Tampa Box Company on 22nd Street.[16]
Almost 500 dwellings in the neighborhood of Ybor City were demolished.[17]
Mt. Zion Baptist Church was demolished in Dade City.[36]
Another church in Dade City was nearly demolished by falling trees.[36]
A turpentine plant in Dade City was damaged, with about one-third of its stored lumber lost.[36]
The Sunnybrook Tobacco Company in Dade City suffered significant impact, with nine large barns destroyed.[36]
In San Antonio and Trilby, a number of buildings were moved off their foundations.[37]
The old city hall in Zephyrhills was moved about 4 ft.[37]
At a hotel in Zephyrhills, the building lost a portion of its roof and several windows were broken.[37]
The hurricane virtually destroyed much of Passage Key, part of which was later rebuilt.[38]
In Lakeland, the school building was deroofed.[10]
Several small buildings in the rural communities outside Lakeland suffered damage.[39]
Nearly all of the buildings at the Pinellas County Fairgrounds in Largo were rendered unusable.[26]
Buildings in Clearwater, including ice and power plants, a theater, and a hotel, were severely damaged; many residences were also affected.[27][28]
Many homes in Oldsmar were practically demolished.[30]

Time_Annotation: The origins of Calasanjy were from the ITCZ in the Mozambique Channel off the northwest coast of Madagascar in early January. On January 9, the MFR classified it as a tropical disturbance, and on January 10, the JTWC designated it as Tropical Cyclone 06S. Later on January 14, Calasanjy made landfall in western Madagascar before re-emerging on January 16 and becoming extratropical the next day.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Later on January 14, Calasanjy made landfall in western Madagascar near Morondava and Cyclone Calasanjy caused heavy damage in western Madagascar.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was first upgraded to Moderate Tropical Storm Calasanjy and then designated as Tropical Cyclone 06S by the JTWC, indicating it falls under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Cyclone Calasanjy produced a peak wind gust of 195 km/h in Maintirano and caused the Morondava River to increase to a flow rate of 2,702 m³/s with a peak height of 4.08 m, evidencing both wind and flood hazards.
